catalog_quote: Mwaghavul has three level tones. The tones are represented as follows; High acute accent above the syllable ʹ Mid unmarked Low grave accent over the syllable ˋ Examples of a three-way height contrast are; high kún three mid kun be old low kùn old age high kús near mid kus to rub together low kùs big ... high sát to say mid sat herself low sàt memorial stone high wáár gruel mid waar to mix flour with water to prepare gruel low wààr law No glides occur on single segments. Phonetic glide arise from sequences of two identical vowels with dissimilar tones and are very rare. They occur principally in a small set of kin terms, some exclamations and borrowed words, mainly from Hausa. Mid tones do not seem to occur on VV sequences, so either HL or LH occurs. ... An important feature of Mwaghavul tone morphology is the use of a tonal change to mark nominalisation.
sweep_summary: Mwaghavul (mwag1236) is in the catalog as 'tonal' on the strength of the Blench et al. 2014 dictionary front-matter phonology sketch (three level tones, minimal triplets kún/kun/kùn). The stress-title sweep produced exactly one item, Pejros 1994 'Some Problems of Austronesian Accent and *T ~ *C' (Oceanic Linguistics 33(1):105-127, DOI 10.2307/3623002, JSTOR paywalled). It is not about Mwaghavul: the Glottolog 5.1 sources.bib entry (saved as glottolog51_ref180954_pejros1994.bib) shows lgcode 'Mwaghavul [sur] (computerized assignment from \"*c\")' against zurichcode 'Austronesian [1]', i.e. the title token '*c' was machine-matched to the ISO code 'sur'; relevance other-language-or-variety, priority none, and it should be removed from the mwag1236 bibliography where it sits as 'Glottolog descriptive ref #7'. Sources already from the 2026-09-16 audit were re-opened at their locators: Frajzyngier 1993 A Grammar of Mupun ch. 1 sec. 4 (tone system; only 'stress' use is the clause-level 'the verb is stressed' register hypothesis, sec. 4.4 pp. 41-42), Akinbo & Fwangwar 2026 NLLT sec. 2.2 (three level tones + LH rising; no 'stress'), Blench et al. 2021 dictionary sec. 2.3.1 (adds rising and rare falling tone), Poret & Punshak 2023 (silent). the PDF is actually Griffin, Akinbo, Ozburn & Fwangwar 2025, PLSA 10(1):5943, doi 10.3765/plsa.v10i1.5943, CC BY) — it reports four contrastive tones (H, M, L, LH rising) plus a phonetically distinct superhigh, mora as TBU, and never mentions stress; it confirms the tonal coding and corrects the wishlist citation. Best statement read: Frajzyngier 1993 sec. 4.4 (clause-level verb-stress hypothesis, no word-stress rule) — corroborates but does not supersede the catalog's deciding source. All fetches and records logged in and in the language folder. Remaining unheld items (Jungraithmayr 1963-64 print sketch; Fwangwar 2018 Ilorin MA thesis) stay low priority.

new_statements.quote: Instead, I would like to postulate that the higher realization of the tone on verb is the result of properties of the clause and not properties of the category verb. In particular I would like to postulate that in the clause the verb is stressed and that consequently all the tones in the verb are realized higher than the tones on the nouns. Thus the low tone is realized as mid, and the mid tone is realized as a high falling-tone. This hypothesis transfers the cause of the raising from the property of the lexical category to the property of the clause.
new_statements.citation: Frajzyngier, Zygmunt. 1993. A Grammar of Mupun. (Sprache und Oralität in Afrika 14.) Berlin: Dietrich Reimer. xiv+538 pp. Open-access scan CC BY-SA 4.0 (digi-hub.de record BV049311587; DOAB 20.500.12854/131913.2).
new_statements.locator: Ch. 1 'Phonology', sec. 4 'Tonal system', sec. 4.4 'An attempt at explanation', pp. 41-42 (scan pp. 77-78)
new_statements.reading: The reference grammar of the Mupun dialect describes a lexical-and-grammatical tone system (sec. 4.1.1 'Tone in Mupun carries both grammatical and lexical functions'; 4.1.2 three phonetic tones h/l/m in nouns, mid/high/high-falling and a few low in verbs) and contains no word-stress or accent section; the only phonological use of 'stress' in the 538-page book is this clause-level hypothesis that the verb is 'stressed' in the clause, offered to explain why verbal tones are realized in a higher register than nominal tones. It is not a lexical stress-placement rule and must not be read as one. It confirms the catalog's kind=tonal coding with word stress undescribed. The 2025 PLSA paper fetched sources in this sweep (Griffin, Akinbo, Ozburn & Fwangwar, 'Tonal alternations in attributive constructions in Mwaghavul', PLSA 10(1):5943, sec. 1: 'previous studies identify four contrastive tones in Mwaghavul: High, Mid, Low, and Rising (Low to High)'; 'we conclude the mora is the tone-bearing unit in Mwaghavul') and Akinbo & Fwangwar 2026 NLLT sec. 2.2 ('Mwaghavul is a tone language... three level tones... as well as an LH rising tone') likewise never mention stress.

sources.quote: 'Mwaghavul is a tone language like all documented Nigerian languages, except Fulfulde (Williamson 1984). The language contrasts three level tones—high (H), mid (M), and low (L)—as well as an LH rising tone.' Instrumental: hummed+spoken monosyllables, 'the four tones have distinct F0 heights and trajectories'; 'the syllable, rather than the mora, is considered the tone-bearing unit (TBU) in Mwaghavul.' The word 'stress' does not occur in the paper.
